questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the phases of clinical trials is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Phase I trials are usually conducted on a small number of healthy volunteers to determine the optimal dose range, assess safety profiles, and detect any potential adverse effects in humans for the first time.

options.label: B
options.text: Phase II trials involve several hundred patients with the target disease and are primarily aimed at determining therapeutic efficacy, while also continuing safety assessment in a slightly larger population than in phase I.

options.label: C
options.text: Phase III trials involve large-scale studies on thousands of patients and are conducted to confirm therapeutic effectiveness, monitor side effects, compare the new intervention to standard or placebo treatment, and collect information that will allow the drug to be used safely.

options.label: D
options.text: Phase IV trials are conducted in patients before the regulatory approval is granted, aiming to determine the most appropriate patient population and help regulatory authorities decide on product licensing.

questions.answerText: Phase IV trials are conducted in patients before the regulatory approval is granted, aiming to determine the most appropriate patient population and help regulatory authorities decide on product licensing.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Phase IV trials are conducted in patients before the regulatory approval is granted, aiming to determine the most appropriate patient population and help regulatory authorities decide on product licensing.

 

Phase IV trials are post-marketing surveillance studies. They take place after the drug has been approved by regulatory authorities and is on the market. They monitor long-term safety, identify rare or long-term side effects, and evaluate the drug’s performance in real-world settings. The description given in Option D mistakenly refers to pre-approval activities, which are actually part of Phase II and III trials.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phase I trials are usually conducted on a small number of healthy volunteers to determine the optimal dose range, assess safety profiles, and detect any potential adverse effects in humans for the first time: True. Phase I trials are the first stage of testing in human subjects. They are typically conducted on 20–100 healthy volunteers (though in cancer drugs, sometimes patients with advanced disease are included). The goal is to assess safety, determine a safe dosage range, and identify side effects.

 

Option B. Phase II trials involve several hundred patients with the target disease and are primarily aimed at determining therapeutic efficacy, while also continuing safety assessment in a slightly larger population than in phase I: True. Phase II trials involve a larger group of patients (typically 100–300) who actually have the disease. These trials evaluate efficacy (i.e., whether the drug works as intended) and continue to monitor safety and side effects.

 

Option C. Phase III trials involve large-scale studies on thousands of patients and are conducted to confirm therapeutic effectiveness, monitor side effects, compare the new intervention to standard or placebo treatment, and collect information that will allow the drug to be used safely: True. Phase III trials are large multicenter trials (often involving thousands of patients). They are meant to confirm efficacy, monitor adverse reactions, compare with standard treatments or placebo, and collect data to ensure the drug's safe use in the general population. These results are usually submitted for regulatory approval.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute-onset chest pain and dyspnea. He is diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction (STEMI) and is urgently started on intravenous nitroglycerin, along with aspirin, clopidogrel, and low molecular weight heparin. The cardiologist explains that nitroglycerin works rapidly through its effect on the vascular system and that care must be taken with dosing. Which of the following statements regarding nitrates (such as nitroglycerin) is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Nitrates primarily cause vasodilation by increasing intracellular nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and increases cGMP levels, leading to smooth muscle relaxation.

options.label: B
options.text: Nitrates predominantly cause venodilation, which reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand, making them useful in angina and acute coronary syndromes.

options.label: C
options.text: Nitrates are known to cause reflex tachycardia due to baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic activation, which can be counteracted by beta-blockers.

options.label: D
options.text: Nitrates should be used cautiously in patients on phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors like sildenafil, but there is no absolute contraindication to their combined use if given 4 hours apart.

questions.answerText: Nitrates should be used cautiously in patients on phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors like sildenafil, but there is no absolute contraindication to their combined use if given 4 hours apart.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Nitrates should be used cautiously in patients on phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitors like sildenafil, but there is no absolute contraindication to their combined use if given 4 hours apart.

 

This is a dangerous misconception. The combined use of nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) is absolutely contraindicated due to the risk of severe, potentially fatal hypotension. Even a 4-hour gap is not considered safe — sildenafil should be avoided for at least 24 hours, and tadalafil for at least 48 hours before nitrate use.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Nitrates primarily cause vasodilation by increasing intracellular nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and increases cGMP levels, leading to smooth muscle relaxation: True. Nitrates are converted to nitric oxide (NO) in vascular smooth muscle, which activates guanylate cyclase, increasing cGMP. This causes dephosphorylation of myosin light chains, leading to smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

 

Option B. Nitrates predominantly cause venodilation, which reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand, making them useful in angina and acute coronary syndromes: True. Nitrates predominantly dilate veins more than arteries, thus reducing preload (venous return), which in turn lowers myocardial oxygen consumption. This makes them beneficial in angina and acute coronary syndromes.

 

Option C. Nitrates are known to cause reflex tachycardia due to baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic activation, which can be counteracted by beta-blockers: True. 
Reflex tachycardia is a well-known side effect due to decreased blood pressure triggering the baroreceptor reflex. It can increase myocardial oxygen demand and is often mitigated by concurrent beta-blockers.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents for routine follow-up. His current medications include metformin and amlodipine, but his BP is persistently elevated at 154/96 mmHg. The physician decides to intensify antihypertensive therapy and explains the benefits of certain antihypertensive classes, especially those that offer renal protection in diabetic patients. Which of the following statements about antihypertensive drugs is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) are particularly beneficial in diabetic patients with hypertension due to their ability to reduce intraglomerular pressure and slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy.

options.label: B
options.text: Calcium channel blockers like amlodipine are effective in lowering blood pressure and are particularly useful in elderly patients, but they may cause peripheral edema as a side effect.

options.label: C
options.text: Beta-blockers such as atenolol are considered first-line drugs in all hypertensive patients, especially in diabetics, because of their favorable metabolic profile.

options.label: D
options.text: Thiazide diuretics reduce blood pressure by promoting natriuresis but long-term use may worsen glucose tolerance and lipid profile.

questions.answerText: Beta-blockers such as atenolol are considered first-line drugs in all hypertensive patients, especially in diabetics, because of their favorable metabolic profile.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Beta-blockers such as atenolol are considered first-line drugs in all hypertensive patients, especially in diabetics, because of their favorable metabolic profile.

 

  • Beta-blockers are not considered first-line antihypertensive agents, particularly in diabetic patients, due to their potential to mask hypoglycemia and worsen insulin resistance.
  • They may still be used in specific situations like post-MI or heart failure, but are not preferred as routine first-line agents in diabetics.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) are particularly beneficial in diabetic patients with hypertension due to their ability to reduce intraglomerular pressure and slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy: True. ACE inhibitors (like enalapril, lisinopril) and ARBs reduce efferent arteriolar constriction, thereby decreasing intraglomerular pressure and reducing proteinuria. They are considered first-line in diabetics with or without nephropathy.

 

Option B. Calcium channel blockers like amlodipine are effective in lowering blood pressure and are particularly useful in elderly patients, but they may cause peripheral edema as a side effect: True. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine) are potent vasodilators and useful in elderly and black patients. However, they may cause peripheral edema due to arteriolar dilation leading to capillary leak.

 

Option D. Thiazide diuretics reduce blood pressure by promoting natriuresis but long-term use may worsen glucose tolerance and lipid profile: True. Thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) are effective in lowering BP and reducing cardiovascular events, especially in the elderly. However, they can increase blood glucose, triglycerides, and uric acid levels.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with a history of non-valvular atrial fibrillation and hypertension presents to the clinic for routine follow-up. He is currently on apixaban for stroke prevention. He reports good compliance but is curious about how this medication compares with older anticoagulants like warfarin. His physician discusses the differences between Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) and Vitamin K Antagonists (VKAs). Which of the following statements about anticoagulant therapy is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor that does not require INR monitoring and has fewer food and drug interactions compared to warfarin.

options.label: B
options.text: Warfarin exerts its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase, leading to decreased synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S.

options.label: C
options.text: The anticoagulant effect of warfarin begins after 4–5 days of therapy, which is why initial bridging with heparin is often required in acute thromboembolic settings.

options.label: D
options.text: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, and its anticoagulant effect can be reversed using idarucizumab in cases of severe bleeding or emergency surgery.

questions.answerText: Warfarin exerts its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase, leading to decreased synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Warfarin exerts its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting vitamin K epoxide reductase, leading to decreased synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S.

 

Warfarin does not inhibit synthesis of clotting factors. Instead, it inhibits activation of vitamin K–dependent factors by blocking vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is needed to recycle vitamin K into its active form. Without active vitamin K, the γ-carboxylation (activation) of factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S is impaired.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor that does not require INR monitoring and has fewer food and drug interactions compared to warfarin: True.  Apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor, does not require INR monitoring, and is not affected by dietary vitamin K intake or many CYP-mediated interactions, making it more convenient than warfarin.

 

Option C. The anticoagulant effect of warfarin begins after 4–5 days of therapy, which is why initial bridging with heparin is often required in acute thromboembolic settings: True. Warfarin’s effect does not start immediately because preformed clotting factors remain active. It usually takes 4–5 daysfor warfarin to exert a full anticoagulant effect. Thus, heparin bridging is often used in acute conditions like DVT/PE.

 

Option D. Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, and its anticoagulant effect can be reversed using idarucizumab in cases of severe bleeding or emergency surgery: True. Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, and idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that acts as a specific reversal agent in emergencies.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old female presents to the outpatient clinic with complaints of burning micturition, frequency, and urgencyfor 2 days. Urinalysis confirms urinary tract infection (UTI). She has no history of drug allergy and is not pregnant. The physician prescribes nitrofurantoin and advises increased fluid intake. During counseling, she asks how different antibiotics work and what their potential adverse effects are. Which of the following statements about antimicrobial drugs is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Nitrofurantoin is commonly used in uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections and is generally avoided in patients with renal impairment due to reduced urinary concentration.

options.label: B
options.text: Fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin act by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, leading to impaired DNA replication and are associated with risk of tendinopathy and QT prolongation.

options.label: C
options.text: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit and are considered safe for use in pregnancy.

options.label: D
options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) acts synergistically by sequentially inhibiting folate synthesis and is commonly used in UTIs, but it can cause bone marrow suppression and megaloblastic anemia in predisposed individuals.

questions.answerText: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit and are considered safe for use in pregnancy.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit and are considered safe for use in pregnancy.

 

Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin) inhibit protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, leading to mRNA misreading and bactericidal activity. However, they are contraindicated in pregnancy due to the risk of fetal ototoxicity (sensorineural hearing loss) and nephrotoxicity.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Nitrofurantoin is commonly used in uncomplicated lower urinary tract infections and is generally avoided in patients with renal impairment due to reduced urinary concentration: True. Nitrofurantoin is ideal for uncomplicated lower UTIs like cystitis, but is not recommended in renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) due to insufficient drug concentration in urine. It is also not effective for upper UTIs or bacteremia.

 

Option B. Fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin act by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, leading to impaired DNA replication and are associated with risk of tendinopathy and QT prolongation: True. Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, disrupting DNA replication. They are associated with tendon rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects, and risk of aortic aneurysm rupture, especially in older patients.

 

Option D. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) acts synergistically by sequentially inhibiting folate synthesis and is commonly used in UTIs, but it can cause bone marrow suppression and megaloblastic anemia in predisposed individuals: True. TMP-SMX blocks folate synthesis at two sequential steps. Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, and sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase. Long-term use can cause megaloblastic anemia and bone marrow suppression, particularly in folate-deficient or elderly patients.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with a history of schizophrenia presents to the outpatient department for medication follow-up. He has been taking risperidone for the past 6 months. His symptoms are well-controlled, but he complains of breast enlargement and occasional milky nipple discharge. The psychiatrist considers modifying his treatment and explains the pharmacological profiles and side effects of antipsychotic medications. Which of the following statements about antipsychotic drugs is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Risperidone can elevate prolactin levels due to dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, causing side effects like galactorrhea.

options.label: B
options.text: Clozapine has the lowest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms among antipsychotics but requires regular monitoring due to the risk of agranulocytosis and myocarditis.

options.label: C
options.text: Quetiapine, while generally considered to have a low risk of extrapyramidal symptoms, may cause QT interval prolongation and should be used cautiously in patients with cardiac disease or electrolyte abnormalities.

options.label: D
options.text: Aripiprazole and ziprasidone are second-generation antipsychotics that are commonly associated with significant weight gain and metabolic syndrome, requiring regular monitoring of BMI and blood glucose.

questions.answerText: Aripiprazole and ziprasidone are second-generation antipsychotics that are commonly associated with significant weight gain and metabolic syndrome, requiring regular monitoring of BMI and blood glucose.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Aripiprazole and ziprasidone are second-generation antipsychotics that are commonly associated with significant weight gain and metabolic syndrome, requiring regular monitoring of BMI and blood glucose.

 

Aripiprazole and ziprasidone are second-generation antipsychotics with a low risk of weight gain and metabolic side effects. Olanzapine and clozapine, on the other hand, are the agents most strongly associated with significant weight gain, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Risperidone can elevate prolactin levels due to dopamine D2 receptor blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, causing side effects like galactorrhea: True. Risperidone blocks D2 receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, causing hyperprolactinemia, which may lead to galactorrhea, menstrual disturbances, and sexual dysfunction.

 

Option B. Clozapine has the lowest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms among antipsychotics but requires regular monitoring due to the risk of agranulocytosis and myocarditis: True. Clozapine is effective in treatment-resistant schizophrenia and is associated with minimal EPS. However, it carries serious risks like agranulocytosis, seizures, and myocarditis, necessitating regular blood count monitoring.

 

Option C. Quetiapine, while generally considered to have a low risk of extrapyramidal symptoms, may cause QT interval prolongation and should be used cautiously in patients with cardiac disease or electrolyte abnormalities: True. Quetiapine has low EPS risk, making it favorable in patients with Parkinsonism or anxiety comorbidity. However, it can prolong the QT interval, especially at high doses or when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte abnormalities.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old female presents with a 2-month history of low mood, anhedonia, early morning awakening, loss of appetite, and feelings of worthlessness. She is diagnosed with moderate major depressive disorder (MDD). Her psychiatrist starts her on sertraline and discusses the general mechanisms, indications, and side effects of antidepressant drugs. Which of the following statements about antidepressant medications is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like sertraline increase synaptic serotonin levels by inhibiting its reuptake, and are considered first-line agents in major depressive disorder due to their favorable safety profile.

options.label: B
options.text: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) like amitriptyline block the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, but their use is limited due to anticholinergic side effects, sedation, and cardiotoxicity in overdose.

options.label: C
options.text: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) increase levels of monoamines by inhibiting their metabolism and require dietary restrictions to avoid hypertensive crises caused by tyramine-containing foods.

options.label: D
options.text: Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor that is frequently associated with sexual dysfunction and is often avoided for that reason in patients with pre-existing sexual concerns.

questions.answerText: Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor that is frequently associated with sexual dysfunction and is often avoided for that reason in patients with pre-existing sexual concerns.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor that is frequently associated with sexual dysfunction and is often avoided for that reason in patients with pre-existing sexual concerns.

 

Bupropion inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake (NDRI). Importantly, it is one of the few antidepressants with a low risk of sexual side effects, and is often chosen specifically to avoid sexual dysfunction, not the opposite. It is also helpful in smoking cessation and can cause insomnia, dry mouth, and anxiety, but not sexual dysfunction.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like sertraline increase synaptic serotonin levels by inhibiting its reuptake, and are considered first-line agents in major depressive disorder due to their favorable safety profile: True. SSRIs increase serotonin availability and are first-line treatments for depression and anxiety due to tolerability and safety, especially in overdose. Common side effects include GI upset, sexual dysfunction, and initial insomnia or anxiety.

 

Option B. Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) like amitriptyline block the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, but their use is limited due to anticholinergic side effects, sedation, and cardiotoxicity in overdose: True. TCAs block NE and 5-HT reuptake but are limited by anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, urinary retention), sedation, and serious cardiotoxicity (QRS widening, arrhythmias) in overdose.

 

Option C. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) increase levels of monoamines by inhibiting their metabolism and require dietary restrictions to avoid hypertensive crises caused by tyramine-containing foods: True. MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase, which metabolizes serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. They require dietary restrictions to avoid hypertensive crisis from tyramine-containing foods.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after experiencing a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting over 7 minutes, with another seizure occurring without full recovery in between. She is diagnosed with status epilepticus and receives the treatment in emergency. She regains consciousness and is stabilized. Her MRI brain is normal. She is otherwise healthy, not on any chronic medications, and mentions that she and her partner are planning pregnancy in the next year. Which of the following is the most appropriate choice for long-term antiepileptic therapy in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Valproate, as it is highly effective across all generalized seizure types and is the treatment of choice for idiopathic generalized epilepsy, regardless of pregnancy status, given its superior efficacy.

options.label: B
options.text: Lamotrigine, which is effective in generalized seizures, including absence and tonic-clonic types, and is preferred in women of childbearing age due to its low risk of teratogenicity when compared to most other broad-spectrum antiepileptics.

options.label: C
options.text: Lorazepam, which enhances GABA-A receptor activity and is the drug of choice for status epilepticus.

options.label: D
options.text: Carbamazepine, which is effective for generalized tonic-clonic seizures and is commonly used as first-line maintenance therapy, with a more favorable teratogenic profile compared to valproate, making it ideal in women planning conception.

questions.answerText: Lamotrigine, which is effective in generalized seizures, including absence and tonic-clonic types, and is preferred in women of childbearing age due to its low risk of teratogenicity when compared to most other broad-spectrum antiepileptics.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lamotrigine, which is effective in generalized seizures, including absence and tonic-clonic types, and is preferred in women of childbearing age due to its low risk of teratogenicity when compared to most other broad-spectrum antiepileptics.

 

Lamotrigine is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and reduces glutamate release. It is effective in generalized tonic-clonic and absence seizures, and carries a low teratogenic risk, making it the preferred choice in women of reproductive age. Slow titration is essential to reduce risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Valproate, as it is highly effective across all generalized seizure types and is the treatment of choice for idiopathic generalized epilepsy, regardless of pregnancy status, given its superior efficacy: Valproate is indeed highly effective for idiopathic generalized epilepsy, including absence, myoclonic, and tonic-clonic seizures. However, it is strongly teratogenic, with risks of neural tube defects, lower IQ, autism spectrum disorders, and other congenital malformations. It is not preferred in women who are planning pregnancy.

 

Option C. Lorazepam, which enhances GABA-A receptor activity and is the drug of choice for status epilepticus: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine that enhances GABA-A receptor activity, and is the drug of choice for terminating status epilepticus. However, it is not used for long-term maintenance due to risks of sedation, dependence, and tolerance. Including it as a long-term option would be inappropriate.

 

Option D. Carbamazepine, which is effective for generalized tonic-clonic seizures and is commonly used as first-line maintenance therapy, with a more favorable teratogenic profile compared to valproate, making it ideal in women planning conception: Carbamazepine is effective for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, but is not effective for absence or myoclonic seizures and may even worsen them. Moreover, it carries a risk of neural tube defects, albeit lower than valproate. Therefore, it is not ideal for women planning pregnancy, especially with better alternatives available.

However, it is not used for long-term maintenance due to risks of sedation, dependence, and tolerance. Including it as a long-term option would be inappropriate. Option D. Carbamazepine, which is effective for generalized tonic-clonic seizures and is commonly used as first-line maintenance therapy, with a more favorable teratogenic profile compared to valproate, making it ideal in women planning conception: Carbamazepine is effective for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, but is not effective for absence or myoclonic seizures and may even worsen them. Moreover, it carries a risk of neural tube defects, albeit lower than valproate. Therefore, it is not ideal for women planning pregnancy, especially with better alternatives available.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male underwent a renal transplant two months ago and is currently on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisolone, and gabapentin (prescribed recently for neuropathic pain). He presents to the clinic with complaints of bilateral hand tremors, occasional headaches, and a feeling of tingling in his feet. His blood pressure is 150/96 mmHg, and laboratory investigations reveal a serum potassium level of 5.9 mEq/L and a rise in serum creatinine from his baseline. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this clinical picture?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Tacrolimus

 

  • Causes dose-related neurotoxicity (tremors, headaches, paresthesias), nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and hyperkalemia.
  • All of these are seen in the patient — making tacrolimus the most likely culprit.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option B. Mycophenolate mofetil: 

 

  • Main side effects include diarrhea and leukopenia.
  • Does not cause neurotoxicity or electrolyte disturbances.

 

Option C. Prednisolone:

 

  • May cause mood changes, hyperglycemia, and osteoporosis, but not typically tremor, hyperkalemia, or nephrotoxicity.

 

Option D. Gabapentin:

 

  • Used for neuropathic pain.
  • May cause sedation, dizziness, or weight gain, but not nephrotoxicity, hypertension, or hyperkalemia.
  • Actually sometimes used to treat tremors, not cause them.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is on warfarin for stroke prevention. He recently started rifampin for latent tuberculosis. After 2 weeks, he develops a new-onset stroke, and his INR is found to be subtherapeutic despite no change in warfarin dosing or compliance. Which of the following best explains the reduced efficacy of warfarin in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Enzyme induction by rifampin leading to increased metabolism of warfarin and reduced anticoagulant effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Enzyme inhibition by rifampin resulting in accumulation of warfarin and paradoxical resistance due to receptor downregulation.

options.label: C
options.text: Competitive antagonism between rifampin and warfarin at the vitamin K receptor, resulting in reduced anticoagulant response.

options.label: D
options.text: Displacement of warfarin from plasma proteins by rifampin, increasing free drug levels and leading to compensatory hepatic clearance.

questions.answerText: Enzyme induction by rifampin leading to increased metabolism of warfarin and reduced anticoagulant effect.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Enzyme induction by rifampin leading to increased metabolism of warfarin and reduced anticoagulant effect.

 

  • Rifampin is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, especially CYP2C9, which is primarily responsible for metabolizing the S-isomer of warfarin (the more potent form).
  • Enzyme induction leads to faster hepatic metabolism of warfarin, lowering its plasma concentration.
  • This results in a reduced anticoagulant effect, causing the INR to fall and increasing the risk of thromboembolic events, like stroke.
  • This is a classic drug-drug interaction that requires warfarin dose adjustment and frequent INR monitoring.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Enzyme inhibition by rifampin resulting in accumulation of warfarin and paradoxical resistance due to receptor downregulation: Incorrect. Rifampin is an enzyme inducer, not an inhibitor. Inhibition would increase warfarin levels and risk bleeding, not stroke.

 

Option C. Competitive antagonism between rifampin and warfarin at the vitamin K receptor, resulting in reduced anticoagulant response: Incorrect. Rifampin does not act at the vitamin K receptor. Warfarin works by inhibiting VKORC1, but rifampin doesn't interfere directly at this level.

 

Option D. Displacement of warfarin from plasma proteins by rifampin, increasing free drug levels and leading to compensatory hepatic clearance: Incorrect. While warfarin is highly protein-bound, rifampin does not significantly displace it. Even if minor displacement occurred, it would increase, not decrease, warfarin's effect — and the liver would not compensate instantly to reduce efficacy to this extent.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with vomiting, sweating, salivation, miosis, diarrhea, and muscle fasciculations after exposure to an unknown substance while spraying his crops. He is bradycardic and hypotensive. On examination, he has excessive secretions, wheezing, and bilateral muscle weakness. The attending physician suspects organophosphate poisoning and begins emergency management. Which of the following symptoms in this patient is most likely due to nicotinic receptor stimulation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Muscle weakness

 

  • Organophosphate poisoning causes cholinergic overstimulation by irreversibly inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, leading to excess acetylcholine at synapses.
  • There are two major receptor types involved:
    • Muscarinic receptors (parasympathetic postganglionic targets):
      • Salivation, lacrimation
      • Bronchospasm, bradycardia
      • Diarrhea, cramping, miosis
    • Nicotinic receptors (neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia):
      • Muscle fasciculations → weakness → paralysis (via NMJ stimulation)
      • Hypertension and tachycardia (via autonomic ganglia stimulation)
  • Thus, muscle weakness is a hallmark of nicotinic receptor overstimulation, and that's the best distinguishing feature in this case.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of hypertension, stable angina, and moderate bronchial asthma is started on a beta-blocker after a recent treadmill test showed inducible ischemia. Within 48 hours, he develops worsening wheezing and shortness of breath, requiring bronchodilator therapy. On review, the prescription reads: propranolol 40 mg twice daily. Which of the following beta-blockers would have been the most appropriate alternative for this patient to minimize the risk of bronchospasm?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Bisoprolol

 

  • Highly selective for β1 receptors
  • Minimal action on β2 → lower risk of bronchospasm
  • Preferred option in patients with asthma or COPD
  • This patient with bronchial asthma developed bronchospasm after being prescribed propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks both β1 (cardiac) and β2 (bronchial smooth muscle) receptors. 
  • Blocking β2 receptors in asthmatics can lead to life-threatening bronchoconstriction.
  • For such patients, a β1-selective (cardioselective) beta-blocker is preferred — especially when there's an indication like angina or post-MI protection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Timolol:

 

  • Non-selective beta-blocker
  • Though often used topically (e.g., in glaucoma), it can be absorbed systemically and cause bronchospasm
  • Not suitable for asthmatics

 

Option B. Nadolol:

 

  • Non-selective, long-acting beta-blocker
  • High risk of bronchospasm
  • Contraindicated in asthma

 

Option C. Carvedilol: 

 

  • Blocks β1, β2, and α1 receptors
  • Useful in heart failure but still blocks β2, hence
  • Unsafe in asthmatics

 

Educational Objective

 

When beta-blockers are indicated in a patient with asthma or COPD, always prefer a β1-selective agent like bisoprolol, atenolol, or metoprolol, and use the lowest effective dose.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is admitted to the ICU with septic shock. Despite adequate fluid resuscitation, his mean arterial pressure (MAP) remains low. The intensivist decides to start a vasopressor to support blood pressure and organ perfusion. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate first-line agent for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Norepinephrine

 

  • In septic shock, systemic vasodilation and capillary leakage cause hypotension despite high or normal cardiac output. After adequate fluids, the vasopressor of choice is:
    • Norepinephrine (Noradrenaline):
      • α1 agonist → vasoconstriction → ↑ systemic vascular resistance (SVR) → ↑ MAP
      • Mild β1 activity → preserves cardiac output
      • First-line vasopressor per Surviving Sepsis Guidelines

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dobutamine: 

 

  • Strong β1 agonist, increases cardiac contractility
  • Used in cardiogenic shock, not pure vasodilatory shock
  • May worsen hypotension in septic shock

 

Option B. Dopamine: 

 

  • Dose-dependent effects:
    • Low: dopamine receptors (renal vasodilation – not useful in shock)
    • Moderate: β1 (inotropy)
    • High: α1 (vasoconstriction)
  • More arrhythmogenic than norepinephrine
  • Not preferred in septic shock

 

Option C. Epinephrine: 

 

  • Mixed α/β agonist, more potent β2 vasodilation
  • Causes tachycardia, arrhythmias, hyperlactatemia
  • Used as second-line or if norepinephrine fails

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of mild Alzheimer’s disease is brought by her daughter with complaints of nausea, diarrhea, and frequent urination. She has been recently started on donepezil by her neurologist. On examination, she is alert but shows excessive salivation. Her vital signs are stable. Which of the following best explains the likely cause of her symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: Excessive muscarinic stimulation due to centrally acting reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition

options.label: B
options.text: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase leading to life-threatening cholinergic crisis

options.label: C
options.text: Peripheral anticholinergic toxicity due to donepezil’s atropine-like activity

options.label: D
options.text: Stimulation of presynaptic muscarinic M2 receptors leading to decreased acetylcholine release

questions.answerText: Excessive muscarinic stimulation due to centrally acting reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Excessive muscarinic stimulation due to centrally acting reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition

 

  • Donepezil is a centrally acting, reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in Alzheimer’s disease to enhance cholinergic neurotransmission.
    • Common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, bradycardia and salivation, all due to excess cholinergic activity.
    • Symptoms are dose-related and typically mild unless overdosed.
    • Unlike organophosphates, donepezil causes reversible inhibition and does not cause irreversible cholinergic crisis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase leading to life-threatening cholinergic crisis: Seen with organophosphates (e.g., parathion, malathion). Causes severe toxicity, including seizures, respiratory failure — not likely in a therapeutic Alzheimer’s dose

 

Option C. Peripheral anticholinergic toxicity due to donepezil’s atropine-like activity: 

Anticholinergic toxicity. Would cause dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, not salivation or diarrhea

 

Option D. Stimulation of presynaptic muscarinic M2 receptors leading to decreased acetylcholine release: M2 receptor stimulation: M2 are inhibitory autoreceptors, their timulation decreases ACh release, which would reduce cholinergic effects — opposite of what's seen here

questions.stem: A pharmacology intern is reviewing autonomic receptor actions to prepare for an upcoming viva. He is asked to match each receptor subtype with its primary physiological action. Which of the following receptor-action pairs is correctly matched?

options.label: D
options.text: Nm receptor – Increased smooth muscle contraction

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) M2 receptor – Decreased heart rate

 

  • M2 muscarinic receptors are located in the heart (SA & AV node). They act via Gi proteins, leading to:
    • ↓ cAMP
    • Opening of K⁺ channels
    • Result: slowed heart rate and conduction

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. α1 receptor – Vasodilation: 

 

  • α1 stimulation causes vasoconstriction via IP₃/DAG pathway and increased intracellular Ca²⁺
  • Used in nasal decongestants, mydriasis

 

Option B. β1 receptor – Decreased renin secretion: 

 

  • β1 increases renin from JG cells
  • That’s why β-blockers lower BP partly via RAAS inhibition

 

Option D. Nm receptor – Increased smooth muscle contraction:

 

  • Nm (Nicotinic muscle type) receptors are found at neuromuscular junctions, leading to skeletal muscle contraction, not smooth muscle
  • Smooth muscle contraction is typically mediated by M3 or α1 receptors

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with complaints of nasal congestion, sneezing, and watery eyes for the past 3 days. She is diagnosed with seasonal allergic rhinitis. Her physician prescribes an over-the-counter antihistamine. Two days later, she returns complaining of excessive drowsiness and difficulty concentrating at work. On examination, vitals are stable and she appears sedated. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Diphenhydramine

 

  • First-generation
  • Causes marked sedation and anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, urinary retention)
  • Diphenhydramine is a first-generation H1-antihistamine that:
    • Crosses the blood-brain barrier
    • Causes CNS depression, leading to sedation, impaired alertness, and psychomotor slowing
  • These effects are undesirable in daytime use, especially in working adults.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Loratadine: 

 

  • Second-generation
  • Non-sedating due to poor CNS penetration
  • Preferred in patients who need to avoid drowsiness

 

Option B. Fexofenadine:

 

  • Second-generation
  • Minimal sedation
  • Ideal for use in professions requiring alertness (pilots, drivers)

 

Option D. Cetirizine: 

 

  • Second-generation
  • May cause mild drowsiness in some patients, but much less than first-gen agents

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with episodic unilateral throbbing headaches associated with photophobia, nausea, and visual aura. She is diagnosed with migraine with aura. She is prescribed sumatriptan to abort her headache attacks. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of sumatriptan in relieving her migraine?

options.label: A
options.text: Dopamine D2 receptor antagonism leading to vasodilation of cerebral vessels

options.label: B
options.text: Non-selective serotonin receptor stimulation causing sedation

options.label: C
options.text: 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of neuropeptide release

options.label: D
options.text: Selective COX-2 inhibition reducing perivascular inflammation

questions.answerText: 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of neuropeptide release
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonism causing cranial vasoconstriction and inhibition of neuropeptide release

 

  • Sumatriptan is a prototype drug from the triptan class, used for acute treatment of migraine.
  • It acts as an agonist at 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors:
    • 5-HT1B: causes vasoconstriction of dilated intracranial blood vessels (especially meningeal vessels)
    • 5-HT1D: inhibits release of vasodilatory neuropeptides like CGRP, substance P from trigeminal nerves
  • This dual action helps relieve both vascular and neurogenic inflammation, which are central to migraine pathophysiology.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dopamine D2 receptor antagonism leading to vasodilation of cerebral vessels: Seen with metoclopramide, used to treat migraine-associated nausea, not the migraine itself

 

Option B. Non-selective serotonin receptor stimulation causing sedation: Too vague and not relevant; sedation is not the therapeutic goal

 

Option D. Selective COX-2 inhibition reducing perivascular inflammation: Describes celecoxib, an NSAID — used in pain but not specific to migraine mechanisms

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman undergoes a normal vaginal delivery, but within 30 minutes develops heavy vaginal bleeding, uterine atony, and hypotension. After initial resuscitation, she is given carboprost intramuscularly. Which of the following best describes the mechanism and clinical use of this drug?

options.label: A
options.text: A PGI₂ analog that causes vasodilation and platelet inhibition to reduce uterine bleeding

options.label: B
options.text: A PGE₁ analog that promotes cervical ripening and delays uterine contraction

options.label: C
options.text: A PGF₂α analog that stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction to control postpartum hemorrhage

options.label: D
options.text: A COX-2 selective inhibitor that reduces endometrial inflammation and promotes hemostasis

questions.answerText: A PGF₂α analog that stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction to control postpartum hemorrhage
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) A PGF₂α analog that stimulates uterine smooth muscle contraction to control postpartum hemorrhage

 

  • Carboprost is a PGF₂α analog used specifically in postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) due to uterine atony.
  • It acts by:
    • Stimulating contraction of uterine smooth muscle
    • Reducing blood loss by promoting uterine tone
  • Given intramuscularly, often after oxytocin failure

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A PGI₂ analog that causes vasodilation and platelet inhibition to reduce uterine bleeding: Causes vasodilation and inhibits platelets → not helpful in bleeding. 

 

Option B. A PGE₁ analog that promotes cervical ripening and delays uterine contraction: Used for medical abortion, cervical ripening, and sometimes PPH, but carboprost is PGF₂α, not PGE₁

 

Option D. A COX-2 selective inhibitor that reduces endometrial inflammation and promotes hemostasis: These inhibit prostaglandins, and would worsen uterine atony, not help

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with a history of chronic gout presents to the emergency department with sudden onset severe pain, redness, and swelling in his right great toe. He has been noncompliant with medications and took allopurinol earlier that day, thinking it would help. His serum uric acid is 9.8 mg/dL, and joint aspiration confirms monosodium urate crystals. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic intervention for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Restart allopurinol with increased dose to lower uric acid levels rapidly

options.label: B
options.text: Begin febuxostat to block xanthine oxidase and halt crystal formation

options.label: C
options.text: Administer ibuprofen to reduce acute inflammation

options.label: D
options.text: Start probenecid to increase uric acid excretion via renal tubules

questions.answerText: Administer ibuprofen to reduce acute inflammation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Administer ibuprofen to reduce acute inflammation

 

  • This patient has an acute gout attack, where the primary goal is to control inflammation, not reduce uric acid immediately.
    • Colchicine, NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen), or glucocorticoids are used for acute flare control
    • Starting or modifying uric acid-lowering therapy (e.g., allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid) during an acute attack can worsen symptoms by mobilizing urate stores and triggering further inflammation

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Restart allopurinol with increased dose to lower uric acid levels rapidly: Can worsen acute attacks. Uric acid-lowering drugs should be started only after acute flare resolves

 

Option B. Begin febuxostat to block xanthine oxidase and halt crystal formation: Same principle as allopurinol — not started during acute flare

 

Option D. Start probenecid to increase uric acid excretion via renal tubules: Uricosuric agent, increases uric acid excretion. Can precipitate or worsen acute gout, especially during an attack

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with morning stiffness, joint pain, and swelling in her bilateral wrists and MCP joints for 3 months. She is diagnosed with early rheumatoid arthritis. Her physician plans to initiate methotrexate therapy, but informs her that another drug will be added temporarily to manage symptoms while methotrexate takes effect. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to provide symptomatic relief during this period?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Prednisolone

 

  • Methotrexate, the cornerstone DMARD, takes 4–6 weeks or more to show clinical benefits.
  • During this time, low-dose glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisolone) are used as bridging therapy to reduce pain and inflammation.
  • Once DMARDs take effect, steroids are tapered off to minimize long-term side effects.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adalimumab: 

 

  • TNF-α inhibitor, used in moderate to severe RA
  • Not first-line unless MTX fails or is contraindicated
  • Costly and immunosuppressive

 

Option B. Hydroxychloroquine:

 

  • DMARD, but takes time to work
  • Not effective alone in moderate-severe RA

 

Option C. Etanercept:

 

  • Another biologic TNF-α inhibitor
  • Not used for immediate symptom relief, and usually reserved for MTX non-responders

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is admitted for worsening dyspnea and lower limb swelling. He is currently on furosemide, carvedilol, and enalapril. His EF is 30%. His physician decides to stop enalapril and start a newer agent: sacubitril/valsartan. Which of the following best explains the advantage of this newer drug combination over ACE inhibitors alone?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases myocardial contractility via β1 stimulation

options.label: B
options.text: It blocks aldosterone synthesis and reduces potassium loss

options.label: C
options.text: It inhibits neprilysin, increasing levels of natriuretic peptides and bradykinin

options.label: D
options.text: It acts as a selective endothelin receptor antagonist to reduce pulmonary pressures

questions.answerText: It inhibits neprilysin, increasing levels of natriuretic peptides and bradykinin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It inhibits neprilysin, increasing levels of natriuretic peptides and bradykinin

 

  • Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) is a combination of:
    • Sacubitril: Neprilysin inhibitor → increases levels of natriuretic peptides, bradykinin → promotes vasodilation, natriuresis, and diuresis
    • Valsartan: Angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) → prevents effects of angiotensin II
    • Superior to ACE inhibitors in reducing mortality and hospitalization in HFrEF (as shown in the PARADIGM-HF trial)
    • Bradykinin levels increase, but less than with ACE inhibitors, so angioedema risk is lower

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It increases myocardial contractility via β1 stimulation: Would increase heart rate and oxygen demand — this is not the mechanism and is actually harmful in CHF

 

Option B. It blocks aldosterone synthesis and reduces potassium loss: Describes spironolactone or eplerenone, not sacubitril/valsartan

 

Option D. It acts as a selective endothelin receptor antagonist to reduce pulmonary pressures: Seen in bosentan, used in pulmonary hypertension, not CHF

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of chronic stable angina is being treated with aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, and sublingual nitroglycerin. Despite therapy, he continues to experience exertional chest pain. His heart rate is 58 bpm, and blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. To avoid further lowering his HR or BP, the physician decides to add ranolazine. Which of the following best explains the therapeutic action of ranolazine in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases coronary blood flow via direct vasodilation of epicardial vessels

options.label: B
options.text: It blocks late sodium current in ischemic myocytes, improving diastolic function

options.label: C
options.text: It acts as a calcium channel blocker that reduces preload and afterload

options.label: D
options.text: It stimulates β2 receptors in coronary arteries, causing vasodilation

questions.answerText: It blocks late sodium current in ischemic myocytes, improving diastolic function
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It blocks late sodium current in ischemic myocytes, improving diastolic function

 

  • Ranolazine is a late sodium current (INa) inhibitor in cardiac myocytes
  • During ischemia, late Na⁺ influx causes increased intracellular Ca²⁺ (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger) → this impairs diastolic relaxation (lusitropy)
  • By reducing intracellular Ca²⁺, ranolazine improves myocardial relaxation and perfusion without significantly affecting HR or BP
  • Useful in patients with low heart rate or borderline blood pressure where other antianginals (like β-blockers, CCBs) are contraindicated

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It increases coronary blood flow via direct vasodilation of epicardial vessels: That’s the role of nitrates or CCBs, not ranolazine

 

Option C. It acts as a calcium channel blocker that reduces preload and afterload: Ranolazine has no significant CCB activity

 

Option D. It stimulates β2 receptors in coronary arteries, causing vasodilation: This would cause vasodilation, but ranolazine doesn’t act on β-receptors

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department with severe central chest pain radiating to the left arm for 45 minutes. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1–V4, and troponin T is elevated. He is diagnosed with an acute anterior STEMI and is prepared for primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). He is given aspirin, atorvastatin, and a loading dose of ticagrelor. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of action of ticagrelor in this setting?

options.label: A
options.text: It irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), reducing thromboxane A2 synthesis

options.label: B
options.text: It blocks platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors, preventing fibrinogen cross-linking

options.label: C
options.text: It reversibly inhibits the P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing platelet aggregation

options.label: D
options.text: It activates protein C to reduce thrombin-mediated platelet activation

questions.answerText: It reversibly inhibits the P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing platelet aggregation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It reversibly inhibits the P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing platelet aggregation

 

  • Ticagrelor is a reversible, direct-acting P2Y12 receptor antagonist
  • It prevents ADP-mediated activation of GPIIb/IIIa, thus blocking platelet aggregation
  • Used in dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin in STEMI, NSTEMI, and PCI
  • Acts faster than clopidogrel and doesn't require hepatic activation

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), reducing thromboxane A2 synthesis: This describes aspirin, which is also used in MI but is not ticagrelor’s mechanism

 

Option B. It blocks platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors, preventing fibrinogen cross-linking: Seen with abciximab, eptifibatide, etc. — IV agents used in cath labs

 

Option D. It activates protein C to reduce thrombin-mediated platelet activation: Not relevant to acute coronary syndrome; related to anticoagulant pathways

questions.stem: A 25‑year‑old woman with no prior cardiac history presents to the emergency department with sudden‑onset palpitations and mild shortness of breath. ECG shows a regular narrow‑complex tachycardia at 180 beats/min. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 98 %. Carotid‑sinus massage and Valsalva manoeuvre fail to terminate the rhythm. She is given a rapid 6 mg IV bolus of adenosine, and the rhythm converts to normal sinus after a brief period of transient asystole. Which of the following best explains how adenosine terminates this arrhythmia?

options.label: A
options.text: Opens potassium channels in atrioventricular (AV) nodal cells, causing membrane hyperpolarisation and transient conduction block

options.label: B
options.text: Blocks fast sodium channels in atrial myocytes, slowing phase‑0 depolarisation throughout both atria

options.label: C
options.text: Selectively inhibits L‑type calcium channels in the His‑Purkinje system, prolonging ventricular refractory period

options.label: D
options.text: Stimulates β₂‑adrenergic receptors in the AV node, increasing cAMP and shortening nodal refractoriness

questions.answerText: Opens potassium channels in atrioventricular (AV) nodal cells, causing membrane hyperpolarisation and transient conduction block
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Opens potassium channels in atrioventricular (AV) nodal cells, causing membrane hyperpolarisation and transient conduction block

 

  • Adenosine binds to A₁ receptors on AV‑nodal tissue → activates Gi‑protein‑coupled pathways
    • ↑ K⁺ efflux → hyperpolarises the membrane
    • ↓ inward Ca²⁺ current → slows phase‑4 depolarisation
  • The result is a very brief (> 6 s) AV‑nodal conduction block, interrupting re‑entry circuits responsible for paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT).
  • Because the effect is so short‑lived, normal sinus rhythm usually resumes within seconds.
  • Common transient side‑effects of adenosine include flushing, chest pressure, dyspnoea, and a sense of impending doom; they resolve quickly due to the drug’s ultrashort half‑life (~10 s).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Blocks fast sodium channels in atrial myocytes, slowing phase‑0 depolarisation throughout both atria: Adenosine has negligible effect on fast Na⁺ channels: its action is confined mainly to the AV node, not the atrial working myocardium.

 

Option C. Selectively inhibits L‑type calcium channels in the His‑Purkinje system, prolonging ventricular refractory period: It decreases Ca²⁺ influx in the AV node, not in the His Purkinje system; ventricular refractory period is largely unaffected.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with no significant comorbidities presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, and occasional syncope. Workup reveals pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) with elevated pulmonary artery pressure and normal left heart function. She is started on bosentan as part of her therapy. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of bosentan in the treatment of PAH?

options.label: A
options.text: It inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, increasing cGMP and promoting pulmonary vasodilation

options.label: B
options.text: It is a prostacyclin analog that increases cAMP and causes vasodilation

options.label: C
options.text: It blocks endothelin-A and endothelin-B receptors, reducing vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling

options.label: D
options.text: It activates soluble guanylate cyclase directly, enhancing nitric oxide signaling

questions.answerText: It blocks endothelin-A and endothelin-B receptors, reducing vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It blocks endothelin-A and endothelin-B receptors, reducing vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling

 

  • Bosentan is a dual endothelin receptor antagonist that blocks both ETA and ETB receptors
  • Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor and smooth muscle mitogen — highly active in PAH
  • By blocking both receptors:
    • Reduces vasoconstriction
    • Slows vascular remodeling and pulmonary vascular resistance
  • Shown to improve exercise capacity and delay disease progression in WHO Group 1 PAH

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, increasing cGMP and promoting pulmonary vasodilation: Increase cGMP, but not the mechanism of bosentan (e.g., sildenafil)

 

Option B. It is a prostacyclin analog that increases cAMP and causes vasodilation: Increase cAMP, but again, not bosentan (e.g., epoprostenol, iloprost).

 

Option D. It activates soluble guanylate cyclase directly, enhancing nitric oxide signaling:  Act downstream of NO but are a different class (e.g., riociguat)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, ischemic heart disease, and CKD stage 2 (eGFR 72 mL/min) is admitted with fatigue, abdominal pain, and mild confusion for 2 days. He was started on dapagliflozin 2 weeks ago as an add-on to metformin and insulin. On exam: mild dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, BP 108/68 mmHg.Lab findings: Blood glucose: 162 mg/dLArterial pH: 7.25Serum HCO₃⁻: 14 mmol/LSerum ketones: ++Serum lactate: normal Which of the following best explains this patient's acid-base disorder?

options.label: C
options.text: Insulin overdose leading to triggered ketone production and metabolic acidosis

options.label: D
options.text: Acute kidney injury causing uremic acidosis and increased anion gap

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dapagliflozin-induced euglycemic ketoacidosis 

 

  • SGLT2 inhibitors promote urinary glucose loss, leading to:
    • ↓ plasma insulin levels
    • ↑ glucagon levels
    • ↑ lipolysis and ketogenesis
  • This can trigger euglycemic DKA (blood glucose often <250 mg/dL)
  • Classic signs: High anion gap metabolic acidosis, positive ketones, and near-normal glucose
  • May be precipitated by stress, fasting, or insulin dose reduction

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Metformin-induced lactic acidosis: Would show ↑ lactate, often with shock or renal failure — not present here

 

Option C. Insulin overdose leading to triggered ketone production and metabolic acidosis: Causes hypoglycemia, not DKA — this patient has normal glucose

 

Option D. Acute kidney injury causing uremic acidosis and increased anion gap: Unlikely with eGFR 72 and no signs of uremia or volume overload

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with metastatic prostate cancer. His oncologist is deciding between leuprolide (GnRH agonist) and degarelix (GnRH antagonist) for hormonal therapy. The patient has significant bone pain and a history of spinal metastases causing intermittent paresthesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate reason to prefer degarelix over leuprolide in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Degarelix is more effective in lowering testosterone than GnRH agonists like leuprolide

options.label: B
options.text: Degarelix provides immediate suppression of LH and FSH without initial testosterone flare

options.label: C
options.text: Degarelix enhances androgen receptor sensitivity, improving response to antiandrogens

options.label: D
options.text: Degarelix has a longer duration of action, allowing once-monthly administration compared to leuprolide

questions.answerText: Degarelix provides immediate suppression of LH and FSH without initial testosterone flare
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Degarelix provides immediate suppression of LH and FSH without initial testosterone flare

 

  • GnRH agonists (like leuprolide) initially stimulate the pituitary → cause a "flare" in LH/FSH → transient rise in testosterone
  • Can worsen symptoms in prostate cancer with bone mets → risk of cord compression or pain flare
  • GnRH antagonists (like degarelix) immediately suppress LH/FSH → no flare → preferred in symptomatic metastatic disease

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Degarelix is more effective in lowering testosterone than GnRH agonists like leuprolide: Both agents achieve similar castrate testosterone levels after ~2–3 weeks

 

Option C. Degarelix enhances androgen receptor sensitivity, improving response to antiandrogens: Degarelix doesn’t enhance receptor sensitivity — it simply prevents GnRH binding

 

Option D. Degarelix has a longer duration of action, allowing once-monthly administration compared to leuprolide: Leuprolide can also be given monthly or in depot form every 3 months - duration is not a major differentiator

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man presents with coarse facial features, enlarged hands, and increased shoe size over the past 2 years. MRI reveals a pituitary macroadenoma. His serum IGF-1 is markedly elevated, and OGTT fails to suppress GH levels. Surgery is planned, but due to large tumor size and invasion into the cavernous sinus, complete resection is unlikely. Medical therapy is considered preoperatively. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for reducing GH secretion and tumor size in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Octreotide

 

  • Octreotide is a somatostatin analog that binds SSTR2 and SSTR5, inhibiting GH release from the pituitary
  • It also reduces tumor size in ~30–50% of cases → often used preoperatively or if surgery fails
  • Best choice when there's mass effect or incomplete surgical resectability

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bromocriptine:

 

  • Dopamine agonist — used in prolactinomas, less effective in acromegaly
  • May slightly reduce GH but not preferred

 

Option C. Mifepristone:

 

  • A glucocorticoid receptor antagonist, used in Cushing’s syndrome, not GH excess

 

Option D. Pegvisomant:

 

  • A GH receptor antagonist, lowers IGF-1, but does not shrink tumor
  • Used after surgery fails and if somatostatin analogs don’t normalize IGF-1

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with complaints of excessive thirst and urination. He drinks 6–7 liters of water per day and wakes up multiple times at night to void. Lab findings: Serum Na⁺: 148 mEq/LPlasma osmolality: 305 mOsm/kgUrine osmolality: 120 mOsm/kgAfter water deprivation test → no significant increase in urine osmolalityAfter desmopressin administration → urine osmolality increases to 550 mOsm/kg Which of the following best explains the mechanism of action of the drug used in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Stimulates V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle to reduce plasma osmolality

options.label: B
options.text: Activates V2 receptors in renal collecting ducts to increase aquaporin-2 insertion

options.label: C
options.text: Inhibits aquaporin channels in the proximal tubule to decrease water loss

options.label: D
options.text: Blocks natriuretic peptide receptors in the distal nephron to retain free water

questions.answerText: Activates V2 receptors in renal collecting ducts to increase aquaporin-2 insertion
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Activates V2 receptors in renal collecting ducts to increase aquaporin-2 insertion

 

  • The patient has central diabetes insipidus (DI) — Characterized by low ADH secretion
  • Desmopressin (DDAVP) is a selective V2 receptor agonist
    • Acts on collecting duct principal cells
    • Promotes aquaporin-2 insertion into apical membrane
    • Increases free water reabsorption → concentrates urine, corrects hypernatremia

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Stimulates V1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle to reduce plasma osmolality: Vasopressin (natural ADH) does this → causes vasoconstriction, not the desired renal effect

 

Option C. Inhibits aquaporin channels in the proximal tubule to decrease water loss: Aquaporins there are not regulated by ADH; and no approved drugs inhibit them

 

Option D. Blocks natriuretic peptide receptors in the distal nephron to retain free water: Natriuretic peptide blockade: Not related to ADH or desmopressin action

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in her first trimester of pregnancy (7 weeks gestation) presents with fatigue, constipation, weight gain, and feeling unusually cold. Her labs show: TSH: 11 mIU/L (↑)Free T4: borderline lowNo goiter or exophthalmosShe is not on any current thyroid medication Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.text: Start propylthiouracil to maintain euthyroidism and protect fetal brain development

options.label: B
options.text: Switch to methimazole after 12 weeks to avoid teratogenicity in early gestation

options.label: C
options.text: Observe and recheck thyroid function in the second trimester as fluctuations are common

options.label: D
options.text: Start levothyroxine and titrate dose to normalize TSH to trimester-specific target

questions.answerText: Start levothyroxine and titrate dose to normalize TSH to trimester-specific target
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Start levothyroxine and titrate dose to normalize TSH to trimester-specific target

 

  • The patient shows classic symptoms and lab profile of overt hypothyroidism
  • In pregnancy, TSH goal is <2.5 mIU/L in 1st trimester
  • Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice — essential to prevent fetal neurocognitive impairment
  • PTU and methimazole are for hyperthyroidism, but are distractors here — the question tests for overgeneralization

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Start propylthiouracil to maintain euthyroidism and protect fetal brain development: Classic distractor; it’s for Graves’ disease, not hypothyroidism
 

Option B. Switch to methimazole after 12 weeks to avoid teratogenicity in early gestation: Also for hyperthyroidism; and even if switching later is standard in Graves’, it’s not relevant in this case
 

Option C. Observe and recheck thyroid function in the second trimester as fluctuations are common: Not acceptable in overt hypothyroidism during early pregnancy

He has no cardiovascular symptoms. Investigations reveal: Fasting glucose: 156 mg/dLHbA1c: 8.2%Serum creatinine: 1.8 mg/dLeGFR: 38 mL/min/1.73m²Urinalysis: microalbuminuria presentLFTs: normalHe is asymptomatic and not yet on any anti-diabetic medications. Which of the following would be the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Metformin – improves insulin sensitivity and delays CV events, even in CKD

options.label: B
options.text: Empagliflozin – lowers glucose and provides renal protection in diabetic kidney disease

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Empagliflozin – lowers glucose and provides renal protection in diabetic kidney disease
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Empagliflozin – lowers glucose and provides renal protection in diabetic kidney disease

 

  • SGLT2 inhibitors like empagliflozin are preferred in diabetic kidney disease (DKD) with eGFR >30
  • They lower glucose, reduce albuminuria, and slow progression of CKD
  • Also provide CV benefit and reduce risk of heart failure hospitalization
  • Empagliflozin is approved down to eGFR ~20–25, depending on the country/guidelines

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents for follow-up. Her medications include metformin and amlodipine. She has BMI of 33 kg/m², and a history of NSTEMI 2 years ago. She reports good adherence to diet but struggles with weight. Current labs: HbA1c: 8.4%eGFR: 62 mL/min/1.73m²LDL-C: 70 mg/dLBP: 128/78 mmHg The physician considers escalating therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to both improve glycemic control and reduce cardiovascular risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Add premixed insulin twice daily to reduce HbA1c more rapidly

options.label: B
options.text: Start glimepiride for potent glucose lowering at low cost

options.label: C
options.text: Add liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit and weight loss

options.label: D
options.text: Start acarbose to slow glucose absorption and reduce postprandial hyperglycemia

questions.answerText: Add liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit and weight loss
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Add liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven cardiovascular benefit and weight loss

 

  • GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) are ideal in T2DM patients with obesity and cardiovascular disease
    • ↓ HbA1c (by ~1–1.5%)
    • Promote weight loss
    • Reduce CV events (LEADER trial for liraglutide)
    • Lower postprandial glucose via slowed gastric emptying and increased insulin secretion

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Add premixed insulin twice daily to reduce HbA1c more rapidly: May control glucose, but causes weight gain, hypoglycemia, and no CV protection

 

Option B. Start glimepiride for potent glucose lowering at low cost: Sulfonylurea weight gain, risk of hypoglycemia, no CV benefit, and β-cell burnout

 

Option D. Start acarbose to slow glucose absorption and reduce postprandial hyperglycemia: Mild effect on postprandial sugars, but modest HbA1c lowering, GI side effects, and no CV benefit

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents for routine follow-up. He has mild cognitive impairment, lives alone, and is on metformin 1000 mg BID with good tolerance. His HbA1c is 8.1%. He denies hypoglycemic symptoms but is concerned about his memory and risk of falls. Renal and liver function are normal. Which of the following oral agents would be the most appropriate to add for better glycemic control in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Gliclazide – Enhances insulin release and has lower hypoglycemia risk

options.label: B
options.text: Pioglitazone – Improves insulin sensitivity and reduces cardiovascular events in elderly

options.label: C
options.text: Sitagliptin – Increases endogenous GLP-1 and has minimal risk of hypoglycemia

options.label: D
options.text: Canagliflozin – Promotes glycosuria and causes weight loss, suitable for elderly

questions.answerText: Sitagliptin – Increases endogenous GLP-1 and has minimal risk of hypoglycemia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Sitagliptin – increases endogenous GLP-1 and has minimal risk of hypoglycemia

 

  • DPP-4 inhibitors like sitagliptin:
    • Are weight-neutral
    • Have very low hypoglycemia risk
    • Can be safely used in elderly with mild cognitive decline
    • Don't impair appetite or fluid balance, unlike SGLT2i or insulin
  • Particularly appropriate when hypoglycemia must be avoided

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gliclazide – Enhances insulin release and has lower hypoglycemia risk: Although safer than glibenclamide, it’s still a sulfonylurea → risk of hypoglycemia, especially in elderly living alone

 

Option B. Pioglitazone – Improves insulin sensitivity and reduces cardiovascular events in elderly: Improves insulin sensitivity, but associated with fluid retention, fracture risk, and potential bladder cancer risk

 

Option D. Canagliflozin – Promotes glycosuria and causes weight loss, suitable for elderly: SGLT2 inhibitors cause volume depletion, UTIs, hypotension → problematic in elderly, especially with fall risk

questions.stem: A 25-year-old medical intern accidentally ingests a large quantity of propranolol (an extended-release β-blocker) during a suicide attempt. He presents to the emergency department 2 hours later with: HR: 38 bpmBP: 74/42 mmHgBlood glucose: 64 mg/dLECG: sinus bradycardia with prolonged PR intervalConscious but drowsy Standard management with IV fluids and atropine fails to improve his vitals. The medical team administers IV glucagon. What is the most likely mechanism by which glucagon improves cardiovascular status in this scenario?

options.label: A
options.text: Glucagon directly activates β₁-adrenergic receptors, bypassing blocked receptors

options.label: B
options.text: Glucagon increases intracellular calcium via cAMP in cardiac myocytes independent of β-receptors

options.label: C
options.text: Glucagon increases insulin secretion, leading to improved glucose utilization by the heart

options.label: D
options.text: Glucagon causes peripheral vasoconstriction through α₁ receptor stimulation

questions.answerText: Glucagon increases intracellular calcium via cAMP in cardiac myocytes independent of β-receptors
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Glucagon increases intracellular calcium via cAMP in cardiac myocytes independent of β-receptors

 

  • In β-blocker overdose, β₁ receptors are blocked → ↓ cAMP → ↓ calcium → ↓ inotropy & chronotropy
  • Glucagon binds to its own receptors on cardiac myocytes, which are Gs-coupled
    • This raises intracellular cAMP → ↑ calcium influx → improves heart rate and contractility
  • This mechanism is independent of β-adrenergic receptors, which are blocked in overdose

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucagon directly activates β₁-adrenergic receptors, bypassing blocked receptors: Glucagon doesn’t bind or activate β-receptors
 

Option C. Glucagon increases insulin secretion, leading to improved glucose utilization by the heart: Insulin secretion does occur, but it's not the rescue mechanism in this context
 

Option D. Glucagon causes peripheral vasoconstriction through α₁ receptor stimulation: Glucagon does not cause vasoconstriction via α₁ — that’s the role of norepinephrine or phenylephrine

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with hypertension and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with a flare of polyarthritis, malaise, and serositis. Her physician decides to start systemic glucocorticoid therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate glucocorticoid to use in this patient that has least risk of sodium and water retention?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Methyl-prednisolone

 

  • This patient has an SLE flare requiring systemic corticosteroids but also has hypertension, so the ideal drug should provide potent anti-inflammatory effects with minimal mineralocorticoid (salt-retaining) activity.
    • Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid
    • High anti-inflammatory potency
    • Negligible mineralocorticoid effect → least risk of sodium and water retention among commonly used systemic steroids
    • Widely used in autoimmune flares, transplant rejection, neuroinflammation, and SLE

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hydrocortisone:

 

  • Short-acting
  • Significant mineralocorticoid activity → ↑ fluid retention, BP worsening
  • Not suitable in hypertensive or heart failure patients

 

Option B. Cortisone:

 

  • Convert to hydrocortisone in the liver, it also exhibits appreciable mineralocorticoid effects, leading to fluid retention.

 

Option C. Fludrocortisone:

 

  • Primarily a mineralocorticoid
  • Used in Addison’s disease or orthostatic hypotension
  • Would exacerbate hypertension — completely contraindicated here
