questions.stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with severe low back pain after slipping in her bathroom. X-ray reveals a compression fracture of L2. DEXA scan shows a T-score of –3.2 at the lumbar spine. She was diagnosed with osteoporosis 2 years ago but stopped oral alendronate after developing worsening esophageal ulceration. She has difficulty swallowing and poor compliance with oral medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her pharmacologic management?

options.label: A
options.text: Give intravenous alendronate to avoid esophageal ulcers

options.label: B
options.text: Start raloxifene to avoid gastrointestinal side effects and improve hip BMD

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate denosumab, a subcutaneous antiresorptive agent effective at reducing spine and hip fractures

options.label: D
options.text: Give methylprednisolone to take care of vertebral fractures

questions.answerText: Initiate denosumab, a subcutaneous antiresorptive agent effective at reducing spine and hip fractures
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Initiate denosumab, a subcutaneous antiresorptive agent effective at reducing spine and hip fractures

 

  • This patient has:
    • Severe osteoporosis (T-score ≤ –2.5 + fragility fracture)
    • GI intolerance to oral bisphosphonates (esophageal ulceration with alendronate)
    • Difficulty swallowing and poor adherence to oral medications

 

  • These factors make non-oral, non-GI irritating therapy essential.
     Denosumab is:
    • A subcutaneous injection given once every 6 months
    • A monoclonal antibody against RANKL → inhibits osteoclast formation
    • Shown to reduce vertebral, non-vertebral, and hip fractures
    • Excellent choice in patients with oral bisphosphonate intolerance

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Give intravenous alendronate to avoid esophageal ulcers: 

 

  • Alendronate does not exist in IV form
  • Only oral formulations are available
  • Zoledronic acid would be the correct IV bisphosphonate if that were the intent

 

Option B. Start raloxifene to avoid gastrointestinal side effects and improve hip BMD:

 

  • A SERM used in postmenopausal osteoporosis
  • Given orally which is not preferred in this patient
  •  Reduces vertebral fractures only
  •  No benefit on hip fractures
  • Also associated with ↑ VTE risk, especially in older women

 

Option D. Give methylprednisolone to take care of vertebral fractures: 

 

  • A glucocorticoid, not a treatment for osteoporosis
  • In fact, long-term steroid use worsens osteoporosis
  •  Would worsen bone loss and increase fracture risk

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic requesting contraception. She is a smoker (10 cigarettes/day) and has a history of migraine without aura. Her menstrual cycles are regular, and she prefers oral contraception. She has no history of hypertension, DVT, or stroke, and her BMI is 23. Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive recommendation for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinyl estradiol + levonorgestrel)

options.label: B
options.text: Low-dose estrogen pill to minimize VTE risk in smokers

options.label: C
options.text: Progestin-only pill (POP) to avoid estrogen-related thrombotic risks

options.label: D
options.text: Emergency contraceptive pill, taken cyclically as primary contraception

questions.answerText: Progestin-only pill (POP) to avoid estrogen-related thrombotic risks
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Progestin-only pill (POP) to avoid estrogen-related thrombotic risks

 

  • This woman is >35 years old and smokes → estrogen-containing OCPs are contraindicated due to increased risk of thromboembolism
  • Progestin-only pills (mini-pills) are safe and effective in this scenario
    • No estrogen = no increased clotting risk
    • Must be taken at the same time daily, but suitable for smokers, migraine patients, and women >35

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinyl estradiol + levonorgestrel): Contraindicated in women >35 who smoke → ↑ risk of stroke, MI, and DVT

 

Option B. Low-dose estrogen pill to minimize VTE risk in smokers: Still contains estrogen → not acceptable in this patient profile

 

Option D. Emergency contraceptive pill, taken cyclically as primary contraception: Not meant for routine use, and not approved as a regular contraceptive

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife due to tremors, restlessness, and confusion. She reports that he had been taking a "sleeping pill" every night for the past 6 months for chronic insomnia, but ran out of his tablets 3 days ago. He now has palpitations, anxiety, and is unable to sleep at all. His vitals: HR 112 bpm, BP 146/92 mmHg, Temp 99.4°F. No alcohol or illicit drug use is reported. Neurological exam reveals coarse tremor and agitation. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for this patient's current symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Alprazolam

 

  • The patient has features of benzodiazepine withdrawal: tremors, agitation, insomnia, tachycardia, confusion
  • Alprazolam has a short half-life and high potency, making it more likely to cause withdrawal when abruptly stopped
  • Symptoms usually start within 24–72 hours of discontinuation

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Zolpidem: Z-drug with shorter half-life, less dependence and withdrawal risk than benzodiazepines
 

Option B. Diazepam: Long half-life → delayed or milder withdrawal, usually does not present like this
 

Option C. Clonazepam: Long half-life; withdrawal is usually delayed and mild

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a 5-year history of Parkinson’s disease presents with increasing involuntary movements, especially after his levodopa dose peaks. He is currently on levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 mg, five times daily. His motor symptoms are otherwise well controlled, and cognition is intact. The neurologist considers adding another agent to manage these peak-dose dyskinesias. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to address this complication?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Amantadine 

 

  • This patient has levodopa-induced peak-dose dyskinesias
  • Amantadine:
    • Is a weak NMDA antagonist
    • Reduces glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity
    • Helps suppress involuntary movements without worsening parkinsonian symptoms
    • Often used when levodopa is optimized but dyskinesias appear
  • Amantadine is the only oral agent specifically approved for levodopa-induced dyskinesias, especially in later stages.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Entacapone: Increases levodopa duration, may worsen dyskinesia, not used to treat it
 

Option C. Selegiline: Boosts dopamine levels, may exacerbate dyskinesia
 

Option D. Pramipexole: Dopamine agonist; helpful in early disease or to delay levodopa, but doesn’t reduce dyskinesias

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with focal epilepsy is started on a new antiepileptic drug after experiencing dizziness and ataxia with carbamazepine. The new drug is well tolerated, does not affect synaptic vesicle proteins or GABA, and selectively enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing sustained high-frequency neuronal firing. Which of the following antiepileptic drugs most likely acts via this mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lacosamide

 

  • Unique mechanism: enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels
  • Distinct from classical Na+ blockers like phenytoin and carbamazepine, which promote fast inactivation
  • Approved for focal seizures, often used in combination regimens
  • Well tolerated; can be used orally or IV

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phenytoin: Blocks fast inactivation of Na+ channels
 

Option C. Levetiracetam: Binds SV2A, affecting neurotransmitter release — no action on Na+ channels
 

Option D. Topiramate: Has multiple mechanisms: Na+ channel blocking (fast), GABA enhancement, AMPA receptor antagonism — but not selective for slow inactivation

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder was recently started on haloperidol. Within a week, she reports feeling extremely restless, pacing constantly, and says, “I just can’t sit still.” She has a history of bronchial asthma, treated with inhaled salmeterol and budesonide. Physical examination reveals no rigidity, tremor, or dystonia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Benzhexol

 

  • This is a classic case of akathisia, a type of extrapyramidal symptom (EPS) caused by D2 receptor blockade.
  • Propranolol is the first-line treatment, but is contraindicated in patients with asthma due to the risk of bronchospasm.
  • In such patients, benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl), an anticholinergic, is a reasonable second-line option supported by clinical practice guidelines and reviews.
  • It restores dopamine–acetylcholine balance in basal ganglia circuits, improving motor side effects like akathisia.
  • In patients with antipsychotic-induced akathisia and asthma, benzhexol is a safer and effective alternative to propranolol.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increase haloperidol: Worsens the problem; haloperidol is the likely cause

 

Option C. Dantrolene: Used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not akathisia

 

Option D. Propranolol: Effective for akathisia but unsafe in asthma

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with a history of treatment-resistant major depressive disorder (MDD) presents to the psychiatry clinic. He now reports intense suicidal ideation, anhedonia, and psychomotor retardation. Due to the urgent need for symptom relief, the psychiatrist considers initiating a rapid-acting antidepressant with a novel mechanism. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug known to produce the fastest antidepressant effect?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Esketamine

 

  • Esketamine (S-enantiomer of ketamine):
    • Administered as a nasal spray
    • Acts via NMDA receptor antagonism → increases glutamate → activates AMPA → rapid synaptic plasticity
    • Produces antidepressant effects within hours to days, particularly useful in suicidal or treatment-resistant depression
  • Esketamine is currently the fastest-acting antidepressant in clinical use and is FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression and acute suicidal ideation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bupropion: NDRI; effective in depression, but onset is delayed (2–4 weeks)

 

Option C. Mirtazapine:  Noradrenergic and serotonergic activity; takes 1–2 weeks minimum to show effects

 

Option D. Venlafaxine: SNRI; standard onset is 2–4 weeks

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unconscious. He was found slumped in his bathroom, with shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils, bradycardia, and a respiratory rate of 6/min. His oxygen saturation is 84%, and he is unresponsive to verbal commands. There is no evidence of trauma or seizure activity. An antidote is administered immediately, with dramatic improvement in both consciousness and respiratory rate within minutes. Which of the following was most likely administered?

options.label: A
options.text: Naloxone – a competitive μ-opioid receptor antagonist used in opioid overdose

options.label: B
options.text: Flumazenil – a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used to reverse sedative effects

options.label: C
options.text: Atropine – a muscarinic antagonist used as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning

options.label: D
options.text: Glycine – used as an antidote in carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning to reduce systemic absorption

questions.answerText: Naloxone – a competitive μ-opioid receptor antagonist used in opioid overdose
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Naloxone – a competitive μ-opioid receptor antagonist used in opioid overdose

 

  • The patient's triad of miosis (pinpoint pupils), CNS depression, and respiratory depression is pathognomonic for opioid toxicity.
  • The rapid and dramatic reversal following antidote administration confirms this diagnosis.
  • Naloxone works by competitively inhibiting opioid receptors, especially μ receptors in the brainstem respiratory centers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Flumazenil – a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used to reverse sedative effects: Reverses benzodiazepine overdose, which causes sedation but not pinpoint pupils or such severe respiratory depression. Also carries seizure risk in chronic benzo users.

 

Option C. Atropine – a muscarinic antagonist used as an antidote for organophosphate poisoning: Used in organophosphate poisoning, which presents with cholinergic excess: salivation, diarrhea, bradycardia, bronchorrhea. Not effective for opioid toxicity.

 

Option D. Glycine – used as an antidote in carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning to reduce systemic absorption: Sometimes used as a local antidote for carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning, but that poisoning causes metabolic acidosis, skin burns, and CNS effects, not the classic triad seen here.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found disoriented and vomiting. He had consumed locally brewed alcohol the previous evening. On examination, he has a fruity odor on his breath, is tachypneic, and complains of blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows optic disc hyperemia. Arterial blood gas reveals a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote to initiate in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Fomepizole – competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase to prevent toxic metabolite formation

options.label: B
options.text: Ethanol – competes with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase, reducing formic acid formation

options.label: C
options.text: Sodium bicarbonate – alkalinizes blood and enhances elimination of formic acid

options.label: D
options.text: Leucovorin – enhances metabolism of formic acid to less toxic products

questions.answerText: Fomepizole – competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase to prevent toxic metabolite formation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Fomepizole - competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase to prevent toxic metabolite formation

 

  • Methanol is metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde and then to formic acid, which causes:
    • Retinal toxicity
    • Severe metabolic acidosis
  • Fomepizole is the first-line treatment:
    • Directly inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase
    • Prevents formation of toxic metabolites
  • Fomepizole is the most effective initial antidote for methanol toxicity.
    Combine with bicarbonate, folinic acid, and dialysis for severe cases.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. Ethanol – competes with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase, reducing formic acid formation: Also competes with methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase Less predictable kinetics, more side effects (CNS depression, hypoglycemia) Used only when fomepizole is not available

 

Option C. Sodium bicarbonate – alkalinizes blood and enhances elimination of formic acid:  Used as adjunctive therapy to correct acidosis Does not stop toxic metabolite formation Helps eliminate formic acid but not a standalone antidote

 

Option D. Leucovorin – enhances metabolism of formic acid to less toxic products: Enhances conversion of formic acid to CO₂ and water Adjunct therapy only, not sufficient alone Used in conjunction with fomepizole or dialysis

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman undergoing a minor outpatient procedure receives a peripheral nerve block with bupivacaine. Within minutes, she develops metallic taste, tinnitus, and agitation, followed by seizures and ventricular arrhythmia. The anesthesiologist suspects local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). Which of the following agents is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Midazolam – to abort seizures associated with LA toxicity

options.label: B
options.text: Amiodarone – antiarrhythmic of choice in LA-induced cardiac toxicity

options.label: C
options.text: 20% Intralipid emulsion – lipid sink therapy to sequester lipophilic anaesthetic

options.label: D
options.text: Atropine – to counteract bradycardia associated with LA overdose

questions.answerText: 20% Intralipid emulsion – lipid sink therapy to sequester lipophilic anaesthetic
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 20% Intralipid emulsion – lipid sink therapy to sequester lipophilic anaesthetic

 

  • The patient has developed Local Anaesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST), most commonly associated with bupivacaine, a highly lipophilic and cardiotoxic LA.
  • 20% Intralipid acts as a lipid sink, drawing the LA out of tissues (especially heart and brain) into an intravascular lipid phase.
  • It is life-saving in cases of bupivacaine-induced cardiac toxicity.
  • In bupivacaine toxicity, administer 20% intralipid emulsion immediately, even before advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) if needed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Midazolam – to abort seizures associated with LA toxicity: Can treat seizures, but does not address the root cause (toxicity)
 

Option B. Amiodarone – antiarrhythmic of choice in LA-induced cardiac toxicity: May help arrhythmias but is not the first-line antidote
 

Option D. Atropine – to counteract bradycardia associated with LA overdose: Useful for bradycardia, but insufficient in cardiac arrest or seizures due to LAST

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy was given rocuronium for muscle relaxation. Patient had developed intraoperative bradycardia and was managed with atropine. The surgeon requests immediate reversal of neuromuscular blockade to secure spontaneous respiration as anesthesia is being terminated earlier than planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent for reversal in this situation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Sugammadex

 

  • This patient presents with two important considerations:
  1. Intraoperative bradycardia, already managed with atropine — so giving neostigmine (which can cause further bradycardia via muscarinic action) is not ideal.
  2. There is a need for rapid and complete reversal of rocuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade.

 

Why Sugammadex is preferred:

 

  • It is a modified γ-cyclodextrin that forms a 1:1 complex with free rocuronium or vecuronium in plasma.
  • Unlike neostigmine or pyridostigmine, its mechanism is independent of acetylcholinesterase inhibition, so:
    • No need for antimuscarinic co-administration
    • No risk of bradycardia
    • Works even in deep blockade
    • Reversal is rapid and predictable

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Neostigmine alone: 

 

  • Causes bradycardia, bronchospasm, increased secretions, unless combined with an antimuscarinic
  • Ineffective in deep blockade

 

Option B. Neostigmine + Atropine: 

 

  • Commonly used, but in this case:
    • Patient already received atropine — further use may cause tachyarrhythmia
    • Neostigmine still ineffective for deep blockade
    • Slower and less complete reversal compared to sugammadex

 

Option D. Pyridostigmine alone: 

 

  • Similar to neostigmine in mechanism
  • Slower onset
  • Also causes muscarinic side effects
  • Not recommended for urgent or deep reversal

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. He is hypotensive (BP 86/50 mmHg) and disoriented. The patient is scheduled for immediate emergency surgery, but his family mentions he had breakfast less than an hour ago. The anesthesiologist wants to use an intravenous induction agent that can maintain cardiovascular stability, preserve respiratory drive, and minimize the risk of aspiration by preserving airway reflexes, especially since intubation might be delayed. Which of the following is the most appropriate induction agent in this situation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ketamine

 

  • The patient is:
    • Hemodynamically unstable (hypotensive from trauma)
    • At risk of aspiration (recent oral intake)
    • In need of emergency surgery
  • Ketamine is ideal in this setting because:
    • It has sympathomimetic effects → supports BP and heart rate
    • Preserves airway reflexes → lowers risk of aspiration
    • Maintains respiratory drive → useful if intubation is delayed
    • Provides analgesia, which is beneficial in trauma
  • In trauma patients who are hemodynamically unstable and have a full stomach, ketamine is the induction agent of choice due to its cardiostimulant properties, airway reflex preservation, and analgesia.

 

Other Option:

 

Option A. Propofol: Causes vasodilation and hypotension, worsens shock
 

Option C. Thiopentone: Suppresses airway reflexes, respiratory depression, and worsens hypotension
 

Option D. Etomidate: Preserves cardiovascular stability but suppresses adrenal function, and does not preserve airway reflexes or provide analgesia

questions.stemHtml: Identify the cylinder shown in the image based on the color coding:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Entonox

 

  • Entonox is a premixed 50:50 mixture of oxygen and nitrous oxide.
  • It is used for analgesia in labor, trauma, and dressing changes, especially when quick onset and offset are needed.
  • The cylinder for Entonox is colored:
    • Light blue body
    • White shoulder
  • This distinguishes it from:
    • Nitrous oxide (solid blue)
    • Oxygen (black body, white shoulder)
  • Entonox = N₂O (50%) + O₂ (50%), delivered as a premixed gas from a light blue + white cylinder, providing rapid-onset analgesia with minimal respiratory depression.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Oxygen: Black body, white shoulder

 

Option B. Nitrous oxide: Entirely blue body

 

Option D. Cyclopropane: Orange (obsolete in clinical use due to flammability)

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman with intermittent asthma uses an inhaler before strenuous activity. She reports rapid symptom relief with this medication. Her doctor explains that it stimulates adenylyl cyclase through Gs protein-coupled receptors, leading to bronchial smooth muscle relaxation. Which of the following drugs acts via the mechanism described above?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Formoterol

 

  • Formoterol is a long-acting β₂-adrenergic agonist (LABA).
  • It binds to β₂ receptors (Gs-coupled) → stimulates adenylyl cyclase → increases intracellular cAMP → activation of protein kinase A → Phosphorylates myosin light-chain kinase and lowers intracellular calcium → bronchodilation within minutes.
  • β₂ agonists like formoterol act via Gs protein → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → bronchodilation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ipratropium bromide: 

 

  • Muscarinic antagonist → blocks M₃ receptors
  • Works via inhibition of IP₃/DAG pathway, not Gs/cAMP

 

Option B. Montelukast: 

 

  • Leukotriene receptor antagonist (CysLT1)
  • Blocks leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction, not G-protein stimulation

 

Option D. Theophylline: 

 

  • PDE inhibitor → prevents cAMP breakdown
  • Increases cAMP indirectly, not by stimulating adenylyl cyclase

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with osteoarthritis has been taking NSAIDs regularly for several months. He now presents with epigastric pain, and upper GI endoscopy confirms a gastric ulcer. He is H. pylori negative and must continue NSAID therapy for joint pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment for his ulcer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pantoprazole

 

  • Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) like pantoprazole are the drug of choice for:
    • Treatment of NSAID-induced ulcers
    • Prevention if NSAIDs cannot be stopped
  • PPIs provide:
    • Potent acid suppression
    • Better healing than H₂ blockers or sucralfate
    • Fewer GI side effects than misoprostol
  • For NSAID-induced ulcers, PPIs are preferred for both treatment and prevention, especially when NSAIDs cannot be stopped.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ranitidine:

 

  • H₂ blocker; less effective than PPIs
  • Many countries have withdrawn it due to NDMA impurity

 

Option C. Sucralfate:

 

  • Mucosal protective agent
  • Less effective than PPIs for healing ulcers

 

Option D. Misoprostol:

 

  • Prevents NSAID ulcers but has poor GI tolerance (diarrhea)
  • Most specific drug for NSAID induced ulcers
  • Not preferred due to adverse effects

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Aprepitant – a centrally acting drug that inhibits substance P at the vomiting center
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Aprepitant – a centrally acting drug that inhibits substance P at the vomiting center

 

This patient is experiencing delayed-phase chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) — typically occurring >24 hours after chemotherapy, especially with cisplatin, a highly emetogenic drug.

 

  • Acute CINV (within 24 hours) is mediated by serotonin (5-HT₃).
  • Delayed CINV (after 24 hours) is predominantly mediated by substance P, acting on neurokinin-1 (NK₁) receptors in the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius.
  • Aprepitant is a centrally acting agent that blocks substance P at NK₁ receptors, which are crucial in delayed vomiting.
  • It is most effective when used in combination with ondansetron (5-HT₃ antagonist) and dexamethasone for cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
  • For delayed CINV, especially with cisplatin, aprepitant or other NK₁ antagonists (e.g., fosaprepitant, netupitant) are the drugs of choice — always part of triplet therapy with ondansetron + dexamethasone.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Palonosetron – a long-acting 5-HT₃ receptor antagonist with high receptor affinity: 

 

  • It is a long-acting 5-HT₃ antagonist and superior to older 5-HT₃ blockers for acute CINV.
  • It offers some benefit in delayed CINV, but not as effective as aprepitant, which directly targets the dominant mediator (substance P).

 

Option B. Domperidone – a peripheral dopamine D₂ receptor antagonist that enhances gastric motility: 

 

  • A peripheral D₂ antagonist, works in the GI tract.
  • Does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it has no action at the vomiting center, making it ineffective in delayed CINV.

 

Option D. Metoclopramide – a dopamine D₂ receptor antagonist with additional 5-HT₄ agonist activity: 

 

  • Works as a central D₂ blocker and 5-HT₄ agonist.
  • Used in mild to moderate CINV or gastroparesis, but is less effective in managing delayed vomiting from highly emetogenic chemo like cisplatin.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is prescribed an oral penicillin antibiotic for a mild streptococcal pharyngitis. His physician explains that this drug is acid-stable, allows for oral administration, but is less effective against penicillinase–producing organisms. Which of the following best matches these pharmacological properties?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Penicillin V 

 

  • Penicillin V is an acid-stable form of penicillin, hence it can be given orally.
  • It’s used primarily for mild streptococcal infections, such as pharyngitis.
  • However, it is not effective against organisms producing β-lactamase.
  • Requires frequent dosing due to its short half-life.
  • For oral streptococcal infections, Penicillin V is used due to its acid stability, but not for serious or β-lactamase–resistant infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Penicillin G:

 

  • Acid-labile, must be given parenterally
  • Also not β-lactamase resistant

 

Option C. Piperacillin:

 

  • Extended-spectrum penicillin, but not orally bioavailable
  • Used IV for Pseudomonas and other Gram-negative infections

 

Option D. Cloxacillin:

 

  • It is β-lactamase resistant, not susceptible
  • Actually acid-stable, used orally for penicillinase-producing Staph aureus

questions.stem: A 72-year-old diabetic man with a long-term indwelling urinary catheter is admitted with fever, chills, and dysuria. Urine culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The physician decides to start an intravenous cephalosporin with antipseudomonal activity. Which of the following cephalosporins is most appropriate in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ceftazidime

 

  • Ceftazidime is a third-generation cephalosporin with broad Gram-negative coverage, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  • It is parenterally administered and used in serious infections caused by resistant Gram-negative organisms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cefazolin:

 

  • First-generation cephalosporin:
  • Good for Gram-positive cocci (Staph/Strep), not effective against Pseudomonas

 

Option B. Cefuroxime:

 

  • Second-generation cephalosporin:
  • Improved Gram-negative coverage, but no Pseudomonas coverage

 

Option C. Ceftriaxone:

 

  • Third-generation, good for many Gram-negative organisms, but not active against Pseudomonas

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with diabetic foot infection is started on empirical antibiotics covering Gram-positive cocci. The resident lists multiple antibiotics that act by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. Which of the following antibiotics does not inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Doxycycline

 

Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic that acts by:

 

  • Binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit
  • Inhibiting aminoacyl-tRNA attachment, thus blocking protein synthesis
  • It is bacteriostatic, not bactericidal
  • It does NOT act on the bacterial cell wall

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Vancomycin:

 

  • Inhibits peptidoglycan polymerization by binding to D-Ala-D-Ala end of cell wall precursors
  • Effective against Gram-positive organisms, especially MRSA

 

Option B. Ceftriaxone:

 

  • A 3rd-generation cephalosporin
  • Binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → inhibits cross-linking of peptidoglycan
  • Used in meningitis, gonorrhea, sepsis

 

Option C. Aztreonam:

 

  • A monobactam antibiotic
  • Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding PBPs of Gram-negative rods
  • No activity against Gram-positives or anaerobes

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis is started on a combination of a β-lactam and another agent that works synergistically by targeting bacterial ribosomes. This second drug is bactericidal, binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit, interferes with initiation, causes misreading of mRNA, and shows concentration-dependent killing. Which of the following drugs best matches this mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gentamicin

 

  • Gentamicin is a 30S ribosomal binder that:
    • Blocks initiation of translation
    • Causes misreading and frameshift mutations
    • Is bactericidal (unlike most other protein synthesis inhibitors, which are static)
    • Shows concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect
  • Often used synergistically with β-lactams (e.g., in enterococcal endocarditis)
  • Gentamicin is one of the few bactericidal protein synthesis inhibitors and is especially valuable in serious Gram-positive infections when used with a cell wall agent.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chloramphenicol: Inhibits peptidyl transferase on the 50S ribosomal subunit; bacteriostatic

 

Option C. Erythromycin: Macrolide that inhibits translocation on 50S subunit; bacteriostatic

 

Option D. Linezolid: Binds 50S near 23S rRNA, blocks initiation complex; usually bacteriostatic (except vs. Streptococci)

questions.stem: A 72‑year‑old woman develops a fever, productive cough, and hypoxia five days after being intubated in the ICU for stroke management. Chest X‑ray shows a new right‑lower‑lobe infiltrate. She was recently on broad‑spectrum ceftriaxone for a urinary infection but received no anti‑MRSA or anti‑Pseudomonal coverage. Her creatinine is normal. The ICU team starts empiric therapy for late‑onset ventilator‑associated pneumonia (VAP) that must cover both MRSA and Pseudomonas aeruginosa until cultures return. Which of the following antibiotic combinations is most appropriate?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Vancomycin + Piperacillin ‑ Tazobactam

 

 

  • Vancomycin covers MRSA reliably in the lung.
  • Piperacillin‑Tazobactam covers Pseudomonas, other GNB, and anaerobes and is standard in empiric HAP/VAP regimens.
  • Together they provide the recommended dual coverage for late‑onset VAP pending culture results.
  • For late‑onset HAP/VAP, start one anti‑MRSA drug (vancomycin or linezolid) plus one or two anti‑Pseudomonal agents (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam, cefepime, meropenem) until cultures narrow the therapy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin: Good for community pneumonia but no MRSA or Pseudomonas activity.

 

Option C. Linezolid + Cefazolin: Linezolid covers MRSA but cefazolin lacks Pseudomonas coverage.

 

Option D.  Daptomycin + Amoxicillin‑ Clavulanate: Daptomycin is inactivated by lung surfactant; amox‑clav has no Pseudomonas activity.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man is started on standard first-line therapy for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis. Two months later, he presents with tingling and numbness in both hands and feet. His liver function tests are normal, and he is adherent to his medications. The physician adds pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to his regimen. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for his current symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Isoniazid

 

  • Isoniazid (INH) is known for causing dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy, especially in patients who are slow acetylators or those who are malnourished, diabetic, or alcoholic.
  • This occurs due to vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency, as INH increases its excretion and interferes with its metabolism.
  • Supplementation with pyridoxine prevents or treats this neuropathy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rifampin: Commonly causes orange discoloration of secretions, hepatotoxicity, and drug interactions, but not neuropathy

 

Option C. Ethambutol: Can cause optic neuritis, leading to red-green color blindness, not peripheral neuropathy

 

Option D. Pyrazinamide: Associated with hyperuricemia and hepatotoxicity

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presents with fever every 48 hours after returning from Odisha. Peripheral smear confirms Plasmodium vivax malaria. He is started on chloroquine, and symptoms resolve. To prevent relapse due to dormant hypnozoites, the physician wishes to prescribe a single-dose agent, but first sends a G6PD test. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for radical cure in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tafenoquine

 

  • Both primaquine and tafenoquine are 8-aminoquinolines that target liver hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale.
  • Tafenoquine has a major compliance advantage over primaquine:
    • Given as a single oral dose, whereas primaquine requires 14 days.
  • G6PD testing is essential before either drug due to risk of hemolytic anemia.
  • Tafenoquine is the only single-dose option for radical cure of P. vivax. Use it only after confirming normal G6PD activity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Primaquine: Effective but requires 14-day daily dosing, not single-dose

 

Option C. Mefloquine: Active only against blood schizonts, no liver stage activity

 

Option D. Lumefantrine: Blood schizonticide used in combination with artemether; no effect on hypnozoites

His physician explains that one of the drugs prevents integration of viral DNA into the host genome, an essential step in HIV replication. Which of the following drugs acts by this mechanism?
questions.solutionHtml:

Option D. Efavirenz: NNRTI; also inhibits reverse transcriptase via a different site

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with prolonged neutropenia after chemotherapy develops fever and respiratory symptoms. CT chest shows nodular lesions with halo signs suggestive of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. While awaiting culture confirmation, the physician starts empirical antifungal therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antifungal agent for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Voriconazole

 

  • Voriconazole is the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis, especially in immunocompromised patients.
  • It inhibits ergosterol synthesis by blocking fungal CYP450 (14α-demethylase).
  • Has excellent lung tissue and CNS penetration.
  • Major side effects: visual disturbances, hepatotoxicity, and photosensitivity.
  • For invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, use voriconazole unless contraindicated; reserve amphotericin B for azole-resistant or life-threatening infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fluconazole: Good for Candida, but ineffective against Aspergillus

 

Option B. Caspofungin: Active against Aspergillus but used when azoles can’t be given; not first-line

 

Option D. Amphotericin B: Active against Aspergillus but more toxic; reserved for refractory cases

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man presents with a painful, vesicular rash distributed over the left thoracic dermatome. He is otherwise healthy and was not vaccinated for varicella-zoster virus (VZV). The physician diagnoses herpes zoster (shingles) and initiates antiviral therapy. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate in this case?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Acyclovir

 

  • Acyclovir is the drug of choice for herpes zoster (shingles), especially when started within 72 hours of rash onset.
  • It is activated by viral thymidine kinase, then inhibits viral DNA polymerase, halting replication.
  • Higher oral bioavailability options like valacyclovir may also be used.
  • Early initiation of acyclovir in shingles reduces viral shedding, speeds up healing, and lowers the risk of post-herpetic neuralgia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Oseltamivir: Used for influenza A & B, not VZV

 

Option C. Zidovudine: An NRTI used in HIV, not active against herpesviruses

 

Option D. Sofosbuvir: Used in HCV; inhibits RNA polymerase, not DNA polymerase

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is undergoing chemotherapy for non-Hodgkin lymphoma. A few days after receiving treatment with an alkylating agent, he develops gross hematuria. Urinalysis shows red blood cells but no infection. His labs are otherwise stable. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for his current symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cyclophosphamide

 

  • Cyclophosphamide is a nitrogen mustard alkylating agent commonly used in lymphomas.
  • It is activated in the liver and produces acrolein, a toxic metabolite that can cause hemorrhagic cystitis.
  • This toxicity can be prevented by co-administration of mesna, which binds acrolein in the urine.
  • Always use mesna with high-dose ifosfamide or cyclophosphamide to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Doxorubicin: Associated with cardiotoxicity, not hemorrhagic cystitis

 

Option C. Methotrexate: Causes myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, not hematuria

 

Option D. Vincristine: Causes neurotoxicity, especially peripheral neuropathy

On examination, Rinne test is negative bilaterally. Audiometry confirms sensorineural hearing loss. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cisplatin

 

  • Cisplatin is a platinum-based alkylating agent used in solid tumors including testicular, bladder, and ovarian cancers.
  • It is well known for:
    • Ototoxicity – irreversible, sensorineural hearing loss
    • Nephrotoxicity – dose-limiting
    • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Ototoxicity is due to damage to hair cells in the cochlea, especially at high doses.
  • Cisplatin’s ototoxicity is dose-dependent and irreversible. Children and elderly are especially at risk. Carboplatin is less ototoxic and sometimes preferred.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vincristine: Causes peripheral neuropathy, but not hearing loss

 

Option C. Bleomycin: Known for pulmonary fibrosis, not ototoxicity

 

Option D. Cyclophosphamide: Causes hemorrhagic cystitis, not hearing issues

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with metastatic melanoma is started on immunotherapy with a monoclonal antibody. Two months later, he develops fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. Labs reveal low T3 and T4, with elevated TSH, suggesting autoimmune hypothyroidism. The drug he is receiving works by enhancing T-cell activity against tumor cells by blocking inhibitory immune checkpoints. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Nivolumab

 

  • Nivolumab is a PD-1 inhibitor (programmed cell death receptor-1) that:
    • Blocks inhibitory signaling on T-cells, enhancing immune-mediated destruction of tumor cells.
  • Side effects are immune-related adverse events (irAEs) such as:
    • Hypothyroidism, thyroiditis
    • Pneumonitis, colitis, dermatitis, hepatitis
  • Used in melanoma, NSCLC, RCC, and more.
  • Checkpoint inhibitors like nivolumab and ipilimumab unleash T cells, but at the cost of autoimmunity. Patients require monitoring for endocrine, GI, skin, and pulmonary adverse effects.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Trastuzumab: Targets HER2/neu in breast and gastric cancers; associated with cardiotoxicity, not autoimmune issues

 

Option C. Imatinib: A tyrosine kinase inhibitor for CML (BCR-ABL); associated with fluid retention, not immune side effects

 

Option D. Bevacizumab: Anti-VEGF agent; causes hypertension and bleeding, not autoimmune hypothyroidism

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is scheduled to receive a new medication. The physician explains the mechanism of action and potential side effects of dutasteride to the patient and his family. Which of the following is true about finasteride?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases the production of testosterone.

options.label: B
options.text: It act as an antagonist of androgen receptors.

options.label: C
options.text: It can cause sexual side effects such as decreased libido and erectile dysfunction.

options.label: D
options.text: It is only effective in reducing symptoms of BPH in the short-term.

questions.answerText: It can cause sexual side effects such as decreased libido and erectile dysfunction.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It can cause sexual side effects such as decreased libido and erectile dysfunction.

 

  • Finasteride like drugs are a class of medications used to treat BPH by reducing the size of the prostate gland.
  • They work by inhibiting the enzyme 5 alpha reductase, which converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). 
  • By reducing the levels of DHT, 5 alpha reductase inhibitors can shrink the prostate gland and improve urinary symptoms associated with BPH. 
  • A potential side effect of these medications is sexual dysfunction, including decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. 
  • These medications can take several months to achieve their maximum effect and can provide long-term relief of BPH symptoms.

  • Epinephrine activates:

questions.stem: A 34-year-old male who completed antitubercular treatment 8 months ago now presents with cough, fever, and night sweats. Sputum culture grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is found to be resistant to rifampicin and levofloxacin, but sensitive to other first-line and second-line drugs. questions.answerText: Varenicline is a partial agonist of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that is used to aid smoking cessation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Varenicline is a partial agonist of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor that is used to aid smoking cessation

 

  • Varenicline is a medication that is used to aid smoking cessation. It is a partial agonist of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, which means that it binds to the receptor and activates it to a lesser extent than nicotine. This reduces the pleasurable effects of smoking and decreases nicotine cravings.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Varenicline is a nicotine replacement therapy that delivers nicotine through a transdermal patch: It is incorrect because varenicline is not a nicotine replacement therapy that delivers nicotine through a transdermal patch. Nicotine replacement therapies include nicotine gum, lozenges, patches, and inhalers.

 

Option B. Varenicline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor that is used to treat depression: It is incorrect because varenicline is not a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). SSRIs are a class of medications that are primarily used to treat depression and anxiety disorders.

 

Option D. Varenicline is a long-acting beta2-agonist that is used to treat asthma: It is incorrect because varenicline is not a long-acting beta2-agonist (LABA). LABAs are a class of medications that are used to treat asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

questions.stem: A patient who is a known case of cirrhosis of the liver presents with abdominal distension and swelling of the lower limbs. The preferred diuretic for this patient would be:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Eplerenone

 

  • Cirrhosis of the liver can lead to portal hypertension, which can result in the accumulation of fluid in the abdomen (ascites) and swelling of the lower limbs (edema). Diuretics are commonly used to treat these symptoms.
  • Eplerenone is a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist that is commonly used to treat hypertension and heart failure. It is also a preferred diuretic for the treatment of cirrhotic ascites due to its aldosterone receptor antagonism, which helps to decrease sodium and water retention.

 

Other Options: 

 

Option A. Triamterene: is a potassium-sparing diuretic that is often used in combination with other diuretics. It is not typically used as a first-line agent for cirrhotic ascites.

 

Option C. Chlorthalidone: is a thiazide-like diuretic that is often used to treat hypertension. While it may be effective for mild cases of edema, it is typically not sufficient for the treatment of cirrhotic ascites.

 

Option D. Furosemide, is a loop diuretic that is often used for the treatment of cirrhotic ascites. However, it is not the preferred diuretic due to its potential to cause electrolyte imbalances and renal dysfunction.

questions.stemHtml: The following table gives the data of AUC of drug A alone and AUC of drug A when combined with drug B. p value is <0.01. Which of the following statement regarding these drugs is most correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Drug B decreases the first pass metabolism of drug A

options.label: B
options.text: Drug B increases the systemic metabolism of drug A

options.label: C
options.text: Drug B decreases the intestinal absorption of drug A

options.label: D
options.text: Drug B increases the renal clearance of drug A

questions.answerText: Drug B decreases the first pass metabolism of drug A
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans A) Drug B decreases the first pass metabolism of drug A

 

  • To interpret the data and determine the correct statement, we need to consider the impact of drug B on the pharmacokinetics of drug A.
  • Comparing the AUC values, we can observe that the AUC of drug A is higher when it is combined with drug B compared to when taken alone. This increase in AUC suggests that drug B is affecting the pharmacokinetics of drug A, potentially by altering its metabolism, absorption, or clearance.
  • Now, let's analyze the statements:
    • Drug B decreases the first-pass metabolism of drug A: This statement is the most correct interpretation based on the given data. The increase in AUC of drug A when combined with drug B suggests that drug B is likely inhibiting the first-pass metabolism of drug A. By decreasing first-pass metabolism, more of drug A is able to reach systemic circulation, resulting in a higher AUC.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Drug B increases the systemic metabolism of drug A: This statement is unlikely to be correct because an increase in systemic metabolism would typically result in a lower AUC, not an increase.

 

Option C. Drug B decreases the intestinal absorption of drug A: This statement is unlikely to be correct because a decrease in intestinal absorption would generally result in a lower AUC, not an increase.

 

Option D. Drug B increases the renal clearance of drug A: This statement is unlikely to be correct because an increase in renal clearance would typically result in a lower AUC, not an increase.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the fastest urate lowering therapy in tumor lysis syndrome to prevent renal damage?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Rasburicase

 

  • Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is a potentially life-threatening condition that can occur in patients undergoing chemotherapy for cancer. It is characterized by the rapid breakdown of cancer cells, leading to the release of large amounts of intracellular contents, including uric acid, into the bloodstream. The elevated levels of uric acid can cause renal damage, including acute kidney injury.
  • Rasburicase is an enzyme that catalyzes the breakdown of uric acid into a more soluble compound called allantoin, which is easily excreted by the kidneys. By rapidly reducing the levels of uric acid, rasburicase helps prevent the formation of urate crystals and subsequent renal damage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A.  and B Allopurinol and Febuxostat: They are other commonly used urate-lowering agents, but they are not as rapid in their onset of action as rasburicase. They work by inhibiting an enzyme called xanthine oxidase, which is involved in the production of uric acid.

 

Option D. Furosemide: It is a loop diuretic and is not primarily used for urate-lowering purposes. It helps promote diuresis and may be used to enhance urine flow in TLS, but it does not directly target uric acid levels.

questions.stem: A drug effect that is produced by therapeutic doses of both nadolol and amiodarone is blockade of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C)  Beta-adrenoceptors.

 

  • Both nadolol and amiodarone are medications that have a blocking effect on beta-adrenoceptors. Amiodarone is a non-competitive beta blocker whereas drugs ending with lol (like nadolol) are competitive beta blockers.
  • Nadolol is a non-selective beta blocker that blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 adrenoceptors. 
  • Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic medication that has actions of all classes of anti-arrhythmic drugs. It is a blocker of Na channels, K channels and Ca channels and it also has non-selective beta-blocking properties.
